Communications may identify the municipality as their source; the operator may identify the federal requirement and criticize the policy. Flexibility and existing materials bear on burden without establishing that every implementation is inexpensive. Materially different messages or burdens remain subject to the same justification, fit and burden limits.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The facial speech rejection is affirmed. The independent administrative remands remain in force.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Glickman supplies the need for an independently justified function and germane communication with criticism preserved; its private-subsidy and attribution conditions retain their own setting. United Foods forbids a chosen message from supplying its own compulsory justification. NEMA's substantial-purpose, practical-fit and undue-burden principles inform this distinct operational application without categorizing municipal outreach as commercial. Barnette and Wooley continue to forbid coerced ideological affirmation or personal endorsement.

For Environmental Defense Center, March 25, 2004, reviewing 344 F.3d 832, see Constitutional Structure for the genuine alternative to third-party administration and Federal Courts: Justiciability for the municipal own-work threshold.

#### Center for National Security Studies v. U.S. Department of Justice (judgment below: 331 F.3d 918) — First Amendment, OT2003

**Docket or dockets:** Supreme Court docket not supplied.

**Decided:** 2004-01-06.

##### Whether the First Amendment requires disclosure of this executive investigative list — Center for National Security Studies v. U.S. Department of Justice, 2004-01-06

**Holding:** A general request for the agency's investigative list does not establish a constitutional right merely because the list identifies detained persons or concerns proceedings to which access may attach. The asserted compilation-access claim therefore fails.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's opinion of the Court, unanimous; all nine participating Justices directly join this proposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The list does not itself constitute the adversarial adjudication to which qualified hearing access attaches. No speech-selected access condition is presented.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Rejection of the independent First Amendment claim is affirmed; FOIA obligations remain separately enforceable.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** North Jersey Media Group’s qualified access to adversarial removal hearings and justified limited-closure safeguards remain intact. United Reporting distinguishes a universal demand for executive information from restrictions selecting access by speech.

#### Leebaert v. Harrington (judgment below: 332 F.3d 134) — First Amendment, OT2003

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** 2004-02-17.

For the other questions in this decision, see Civil Rights — whether parental educational liberty requires an exemption from neutral compulsory instruction.

##### Whether combining parental and religious objections establishes heightened scrutiny of ordinary instruction — Leebaert v. Harrington, 2004-02-17

**Holding:** A religious objection to public-school instruction requires its own examination of protected religious interference; adding a parental-liberty label does not supply elements missing from either claim or itself require heightened scrutiny. Neutral ordinary instruction remains distinct from compelled professions of belief, religious targeting and discriminatory treatment.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** The stipulated attendance record establishes no compelled belief, targeting or discriminatory treatment. It does not show the distinctive interference with religious life and parental direction underlying Yoder; the religion's age, size or popularity does not determine sufficiency.

**Limits and questions not reached:** An educational label cannot insulate actual coercion or religious discrimination. The decision does not categorically resolve every possible combined-rights theory.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The federal religious-exercise claim remains dismissed; the state-law dismissal remains without prejudice.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Wisconsin v. Yoder is distinguished by the protected interference present there. Employment Division v. Smith and Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah retain their respective neutral-rule and religious-targeting rules. Shahar v. Bowers and Curtis preserve independent consideration of religious exercise; Brown's earlier procedural treatment of free exercise supplies no new merits rule.

#### Locke v. Davey, 540 U.S. 712

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-1315.
**Decided:** 2004-02-25.

##### Whether Washington may exclude the devotional ministry degree from its individual scholarship — Locke v. Davey, 2004-02-25

**Holding:** The Free Exercise Clause permits Washington's confined exclusion of a devotional degree preparing a student for ministry from the individual scholarship at issue, while the program continues to admit religious students and institutions, individual theology courses and eligible secular courses of study. That permission does not authorize disqualification merely for religious belief, affiliation or an isolated theology course.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter's opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer: five direct joins to the complete permission rule and remedy. Stone-Zsela supplies a sixth vote for reversal concerning pastoral formation on a distinct ground, not a join to this rationale.

**Material application:** The award passes through the institution to the student for tuition, living and other educational expenses. The parties agree that the theology-degree condition addresses devotional study or study designed to induce faith, and Davey's pastoral training falls within it. A concurrent business major does not transform this award into a restricted secular-department grant; the program permits support for a secular degree at another institution while devotional study occurs elsewhere.

**Limits and questions not reached:** This is permission to decline the identified ministry support, not an Establishment Clause duty to exclude it or a finding that each dollar purchases devotion. The grant resolves the Free Exercise claim only.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Pastoral-degree payment refusal is sustained through reversal, 6–3. The five opinion joiners restore Washington's favorable judgment without the proposed secular-component remand, 5–4; the four opposing that restoration do not share a single alternative remedy.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Walz v. Tax Commission recognizes permissible separation beyond constitutional prohibition. Witters preserves individual vocational aid without compelling every devotional subsidy. Strout and Zelman retain their rules for different integrated or restricted purchases. Agostini retains actual-function analysis. K.D.M. and Columbia Union retain equality for independently identifiable secular work. Lukumi's targeting rule is distinguished from this bounded ministry-support choice.

#### Freedom From Religion Foundation, Inc. v. McCallum (judgment below: 324 F.3d 880) — First Amendment, OT2003

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied; Seventh Circuit No. 02-3102.
**Decided:** 2004-02-26.

For the other questions in this decision, see Federal Courts: Justiciability — whether the identified correctional-contract expenditure supports taxpayer standing; Federal Courts: Immunities and Remedies — whether prospective relief must stop each proved devotional payment while preserving separated secular services.

##### Whether voluntary provider selection validates restricted payments buying integrated religious treatment — Freedom From Religion Foundation, Inc. v. McCallum, 2004-02-26

**Holding:** Government may not purchase devotional formation integrated into rehabilitation through restricted contract payments merely because the offender voluntarily selected a provider and had a secular alternative. The claimant must prove the religious function actually financed; religious affiliation, other institutional religious activity or speculative freeing of resources does not suffice, while identifiable secular services remain eligible with documented operational separation and reliable accounting.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** Wisconsin reimburses a selected contracted provider for part of placement costs rather than distributing an unrestricted personal grant to the offender. The secular rehabilitative objective and accepted findings of nonbinding recommendations, secular alternatives and no religious favoritism do not answer what the State buys.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The record leaves cost categories, secular-use restrictions and full separation scope for application below. Neither complete devotional financing nor exclusively secular reimbursement may be presumed. Greater program attractiveness alone does not overturn the accepted noncoercion findings.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The choice-only sustainment is reversed, with application to the existing trial record and additional findings only for material application gaps. The separate Workforce Development judgment remains undisturbed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Agostini supplies unified governmental-function analysis; Mitchell requires actual-use proof. Strout and Zelman extend to analogous restricted correctional-service purchases. Columbia Union and K.D.M. preserve reliably separated secular eligibility. Locke and Witters retain their distinct individual-assistance relationships. Lee v. Weisman retains its coercion inquiry, which does not exhaust the financing issue.



### Prison religious diets

#### Williams v. Morton

**Docket or dockets:** No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied.
**Decided:** 2004-06-02

For Williams v. Morton, 2004-06-02, No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied, see Civil Rights for [The asserted meat-based comparator lacks its factual predicate](../HOLDINGS.md#the-asserted-meat-based-comparator-lacks-its-factual-predicate).

##### The governing constitutional and summary-judgment standards

**Holding:** A prison restriction on sincere religious exercise must bear a reasonable relationship to legitimate, neutral penological objectives under Turner, considering the actual alternatives for exercise, the institutional consequences of accommodation and ready alternatives. Prisoners retain the ultimate burden to show unreasonableness, while officials seeking summary judgment must establish the absence of a genuine dispute over facts material to that inquiry.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part I, joined by all nine Justices, is the opinion of the Court.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The standard does not require the least restrictive means. Sincerity does not require proof that every adherent shares the obligation. The contamination claim was voluntarily dismissed; no preserved RLUIPA claim or late-witness ruling is presented.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Turner supplies the four-factor reasonable-relationship standard; O’Lone applies it to prison religious exercise; Overton preserves supported operational objectives, actual alternatives and the prisoner’s ultimate burden.

##### The record supports the refusal to add halal meat

**Holding:** The supplied meal-administration, screening, cost and program-scale evidence establishes a reasonable relationship between this diet policy and legitimate prison objectives. Evidence that outside vendors could supply halal meat does not create a material dispute defeating summary judgment when it leaves those sufficient operational grounds intact and does not establish an equally effective alternative at negligible institutional cost.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part II, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer, controls by eight direct joins.

**Material application:** The proposed program covered approximately 225 prisoners, compared with four receiving kosher meals. Possible vendor supply left the supported administration, screening, scale and added-expense concerns intact. Other actual religious opportunities matter without replacing the diet inquiry.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Added cost alone does not categorically answer a sincere religious-exercise claim.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Summary judgment for officials is affirmed on Free Exercise, 8–1; the requested meal order and damages on that claim are denied.

### Judicial timing in adult-business licensing

#### City of Littleton v. Z. J. Gifts D-4, L.L.C., 541 U.S. 774

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-1609.
**Decided:** 2004-06-07

##### Judicial review must protect against suppression through delay

**Holding:** An adult-business licensing scheme governing protected expression must assure a judicial determination promptly enough to prevent delay from suppressing that expression. Prompt access to file a challenge alone does not satisfy this requirement if the challenged restraint can remain effective indefinitely without a decision.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's Part I is joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Those seven direct joins make it controlling.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The seven-Justice prompt-determination rule does not impose Freedman’s entire direct-censorship procedure on objective licensing.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** - FW/PBS, Inc. v. Dallas is clarified: the core protection against licensing delay extends to judicial determination, while ordinary procedures can supply effective protection in this objective scheme.
- Thomas v. Chicago Park District is extended to the judicial-timing issue it reserved. Its distinction between objective administration and the complete censorship procedure remains effective.
- Freedman v. Maryland is distinguished as direct censorship; its stronger procedural safeguards continue to govern that setting.

##### Effective ordinary procedures satisfy this facial challenge

**Holding:** An objective, nondiscretionary adult-business licensing scheme need not prescribe a special fixed judicial deadline when existing court procedures provide effective expedition and interim protection against suppression through delay. Colorado's identified ordinary procedures satisfy that facial requirement on this record; courts must use their available tools when delay threatens significant First Amendment injury.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's Part II is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Thomas and Ginsburg. Those six direct joins make its rationale and application controlling.

**Material application:** Objective qualifications permit relatively prompt resolution, and Colorado supplies expedition and interim-relief procedures. The bookstore never applied for a license and presents no actual delayed appeal.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The facial judicial-timing ruling is reversed unanimously and remanded. The ordinance survives this objection, but courts must employ expedition or interim protection where concrete delay threatens protected expression.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Part II has six direct joins; the judgment’s unanimity does not make every separate adequacy theory controlling. Content censorship retains Freedman’s stronger safeguards.

### Adult Internet speech, filtering alternatives and preliminary relief

#### Ashcroft v. American Civil Liberties Union, 542 U.S. 656

**Docket or dockets:** No. 03-218.
**Decided:** June 29, 2004.

##### How the complete content-based restriction must be compared with concrete less restrictive alternatives

**Holding:** When a content-based restriction burdens protected adult Internet expression and a concrete, plausibly effective less restrictive alternative is identified, the Government must establish why that alternative's comparative inadequacy warrants the broader restriction in serving the compelling child-protection interest. At the preliminary stage, an injunction may remain when the supported record shows a likelihood that the Government cannot meet that burden and the other equitable requirements are satisfied; appellate review respects the district court's discretion while independently correcting legal error.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Ginsburg's opinion, joined by all nine Justices, supplies the common framework.

**Material statutory scope:** The earlier Ashcroft decision requires the statute to be considered as a whole. COPA reaches knowing World Wide Web communications in interstate or foreign commerce, made for commercial purposes with knowledge of their character, available to persons under seventeen and harmful to minors. Its commercial category concerns a regular business course and profit objective, with knowing posting or solicitation; it requires neither actual profit nor a sole or principal business. That category does not turn protected literature into commercial advertising.

Harmful material is obscenity or material satisfying all three additional elements: taken as a whole, prurient appeal or pandering with respect to minors under contemporary community standards; specified patently offensive sexual depictions, descriptions or representations with respect to minors; and, taken as a whole, lack of serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value for minors. The content element includes actual or simulated sexual acts or contacts and lewd displays of genitals or post-pubescent female breasts. The community-standards language expressly appears in the prurience element; serious value remains objective under Pope v. Illinois.

Section 231(b) excludes telecommunications carriers, Internet-access providers and information-location services to the extent they act in those capacities. It separately protects intermediaries transmitting, storing, retrieving, hosting, formatting or translating another's communication without selecting or altering its content; deletion consistent with §231(c) or §230 does not defeat that protection. Section 231(c)(1)'s alternative good-faith access defenses are credit card or debit account use, adult access code or adult personal identification number, an age-verifying digital certificate, or other reasonable measures feasible with available technology. Section 231(c)(2) separately protects good-faith implementation or restriction activity against a cause of action only if the activity violates no law carrying a criminal or civil penalty. Section 231(d) requires protection against unauthorized access to collected information and prior written or electronic consent for disclosure from the adult concerned or the parent or guardian of a person under seventeen; disclosure is permitted when necessary to communicate, to conduct legitimate related business activity, or under an authorizing court order. These provisions protect information without guaranteeing absolute anonymity.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The commercial category does not convert protected literature into commercial advertising, and lack of serious value for minors does not remove adult protection. Defenses and privacy provisions reduce coverage and potential liability without establishing affordable, anonymous and effective access for every adult. Legislative predictions receive serious consideration; neither an imagined alternative nor a demand for perfect filtering resolves the comparison.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** - Ashcroft v. American Civil Liberties Union, 535 U.S. 564, is applied: rejection of community standards as an automatic ground of invalidity requires integrated review and preserves consideration of actual adult burdens.
- Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union is applied to protected adult Internet access, workable safeguards and genuine textual severance; COPA's different elements receive their own examination.
- United States v. Playboy Entertainment Group is applied to the Government's comparative justification burden and the need for concrete alternatives rather than perfect protection.
- Pope v. Illinois is applied to the objective serious-value inquiry; community approval does not supply that element.

##### Whether the filtering comparison supports continued preliminary protection and what final adjudication requires

**Holding:** The district court did not abuse its discretion by preserving the injunction because the supported comparison shows a likelihood that the Government cannot justify COPA's adult-speech burdens against user-controlled filtering. The injunction continues while the district court promptly resolves final validity through the integrated statutory inquiry; supported findings remain unless genuinely new evidence or legal error warrants reconsideration, and challengers need not disprove every conceivable alternative.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Ginsburg's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg, controls by six direct joins.

**Material application:** Receiving-end filters can reach foreign-origin and non-Web material beyond COPA while allowing adults to choose lawful reading. The Government's proof did not adequately justify the broader adult burdens despite COPA's additional protection where household filters are not activated. The comparison assumes neither universal parental participation nor flawless filtering.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Final facial validity and supported particular applications require the merits record. Genuine new evidence or legal error may justify reconsideration of supported findings. Any severance must correspond to an actual statutory division rather than create a new offense.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The Attorney General remains bound by the existing injunction without an enforcement gap. It must prevent the demonstrated chilling and access burdens; a narrower order requires a supported showing that it would provide an effective cure. Modification requires a supported legal or factual basis. The preliminary injunction remains continuously effective. The district court must proceed promptly under the complete statutory and comparative inquiry, identify material disputed updated facts and specify the scope and any genuine severance in its final order. A supported change to relief must preserve an effective cure for demonstrated speech burdens.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** - United States v. American Library Association is distinguished at its library-service, funding and effective-access scope. Its distinct statutory disabling provisions retain their own terms.

## Standards and Tests selection: One-year state-custody habeas filing period

### One-year state-custody habeas filing period

**Governing question:** The limitation period under amended §2244(d).

**Current rule:** A person in custody pursuant to a state-court judgment has one year to apply for habeas relief, running from the latest of: finality by completion of direct review or expiration of time to seek it; removal of a State-created filing impediment violating federal law that actually prevented filing; initial Supreme Court recognition of the asserted constitutional right, if newly recognized and made retroactively applicable on collateral review; or when due diligence could have discovered the claim’s factual predicate. Time during which a properly filed application for state postconviction or other collateral review of the pertinent judgment or claim is pending is excluded.

Proper filing concerns compliance with requirements for delivery and acceptance of the application, rather than the success or relief eligibility of its individual claims. Claim-relief bars therefore do not invalidate an otherwise proper filing. Clerk acceptance cannot cure a genuine filing defect. Form, deadlines, the proper receiving court or office, fees and filing preconditions must be distinguished from rules requiring denial of relief on a claim.

The state-proceeding limitation applies to both postconviction review and other collateral review. Pendency of a federal habeas application is not excluded under section 2244(d)(2), even if that application was timely and dismissed without prejudice for unestablished exhaustion. Accompanying civil-rights allegations do not convert it into state review. A later application's non-successive status and an earlier application's timely filing do not themselves make the later application timely; proper filing, actual pendency and relation to the pertinent judgment or claim remain independent conditions.

A properly filed state collateral application remains pending through timely continuation of the ordinary state-review process, including qualifying intervals before filing at the next available level. Successive-level original petitions qualify when they perform that review function. Completion, abandonment, an unreasonable interval or an unrelated later attack does not receive exclusion merely because another petition is possible. A state merits discussion does not override an independent valid untimeliness determination. Where the order is ambiguous, the federal court must determine its actual meaning, the applicable state timing rule, the supported explanation for the interval and elapsed time; lawful clarification may be used but is not invariably required. No national fixed deadline or automatic reasonableness presumption applies.

**Authority by component:**

- Four alternative latest-event triggers and pending-state-review exclusion: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §101, 28 U.S.C. §2244(d), enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

- Proper application filing distinguished from claim-relief bars: Canonical Decision Record `Artuz_v_Bennett_merits_2000-11-07.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Filing an application is distinct from entitlement to relief on its claims, 2000-11-07; Ginsburg for all nine Justices.
- State-only collateral pendency, independent timing and preservation of actual alternative grounds: Canonical Decision Record `Duncan_v_Walker_merits_2001-06-18.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / 1. Federal habeas pendency is outside section 2244(d)(2); 2. The statutory error requires reversal, with actual independent alternatives preserved, 2001-06-18; seven direct joins to O’Connor’s opinion.

- Canonical Decision Record `carey-v-saffold_merits_2002-06-17.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Timely ordinary state review includes its intervals; State timeliness and the actual federal calculation remain necessary; June 17, 2002; Ginsburg with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer (six direct joins).

**Present operation effective:** Carey v. Saffold, June 17, 2002, for ordinary-review interval pendency and state-timeliness limits. Duncan, Artuz and the enacted commencement triggers retain their earlier effective dates and distinct functions.

**Effective transition:** Enacted April 24, 1996. “Temporal reach of ordinary AEDPA habeas amendments” states Lindh's noncapital chapter 153 application-date construction, effective 1997-06-23. Separately directed provisions, chapter 154's express pending-case clause and Felker's successive-petition treatment remain distinct; Lindh does not settle every other Title I provision's application to pending proceedings. Authority: Lindh v. Murphy — The chapter 153 amendments at issue do not govern this pre-enactment noncapital application, Ginsburg's six-Justice opinion, 1997-06-23.

**Holdings navigation:** Lindh v. Murphy (1997-06-23) — The chapter 153 amendments at issue do not govern this pre-enactment noncapital application. [Artuz v. Bennett, 531 U.S. 4 — Habeas limitations and state collateral review](HOLDINGS.md#artuz-v-bennett-531-us-4); [Duncan v. Walker, 533 U.S. 167 — Federal habeas pendency and statutory limitation periods](HOLDINGS.md#duncan-v-walker-533-us-167).

**Open question:** Artuz leaves unresolved whether an exception to a filing deadline can make a late application properly filed. Duncan’s equity reservation is resolved only for the defined court-created impediments governed by “Court-directed mixed-petition elections and loss of timely review,” under Pliler v. Ford, June 21, 2004. General mixed-petition stay authority remains unresolved. Preserved, legally available commencement or equitable grounds require their own actual predicates; neither an automatic extension nor categorical foreclosure follows. Section 2254(b)(2) permits, but does not require, merits denial of an unexhausted application.


**Related current rules:** “Court-directed mixed-petition elections and loss of timely review” supplies the separate notice, causal-loss, diligence and lawful-remedy requirements. [Pliler v. Ford — Parts I–IV](../terms/OT2003/records/pliler_v_ford_merits_2004-06-21.md#holdings) does not change the statutory exclusion of federal pendency or the earlier commencement and state-pendency dates.

## Standards and Tests selection: Convicting-jurisdiction law for the firearms conviction exclusion

### Convicting-jurisdiction law for the firearms conviction exclusion

**Governing question:** Which jurisdiction's law governs whether expungement, set-aside, pardon or restoration of civil rights excludes a conviction under 18 U.S.C. §921(a)(20) for the federal firearms prohibition.

**Current rule:** Apply the law of the jurisdiction where the proceedings occurred to the related conviction exclusion for expungement, set-aside, pardon or restoration of civil rights. State restoration alone does not remove a federal conviction as a §922(g) predicate. The enacted exclusion retains its qualification: a conviction is not excluded if the pardon, expungement or restoration of civil rights expressly provides that the person may not ship, transport, possess, or receive firearms. State administration of ordinary civil rights and difficulty obtaining federal relief do not supply a different sovereign selector or create a judicial restoration procedure. Where civil rights are restored but a substantial express firearm disability remains, including a prohibition on handgun possession outside home or business, the conviction remains a federal predicate even for rifles or shotguns the State permits. Each federal offense or enhancement still requires proof of its own conditions.

**Authority by component:**

- Convicting-sovereign selector and retained-firearms qualification: Beecham and Jones — The law of the convicting jurisdiction governs the conviction exclusion, 1994-05-16. O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; unanimous direct support.

- Caron: continuing substantial firearms restriction and conviction-wide federal effect: Caron v. United States, No. 97-6270. — controlling Holdings, 1998-06-22.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-06-22, for the new component; earlier component authorities retain their stated dates.

**Open question:** The decision does not establish the availability or satisfaction of a particular federal pardon or restoration mechanism, §925(c) relief, the required civil-rights bundle, automatic versus affirmative restoration, or federal habeas as a set-aside.

**Related current rules:** Collateral attacks on state predicates at federal sentencing and under section 2255 governs the distinct sentencing-forum question; it does not replace this conviction-selector rule.

**Holdings navigation:** The law of the convicting jurisdiction governs the conviction exclusion. Caron v. United States, 524 U.S. 308 — Restored civil rights and federal firearms predicates.

## Standards and Tests selection: Materiality in financial-deception fraud schemes

### Materiality in financial-deception fraud schemes

**Governing question:** Whether mail, wire and bank fraud require material representations and what materiality means.

**Current rule:** Materiality is an element of the charged money-or-property financial-deception schemes under §§1341 and 1343 and the charged bank-fraud schemes under §1344. In transaction context, a representation is material when it has a natural tendency or capacity to influence its targeted decision. Successful deception, actual reliance, actual loss and status as the sole reason for the transaction are unnecessary. Mail or wire use remains separate and may execute the scheme without itself containing the falsehood.

**Authority by component:**

- Neder v. United States — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “I. Materiality in the charged mail, wire, and bank fraud schemes”, 1999-06-10; Thomas Part I, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Neder, June 10, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** Both §1344 routes retain materiality for the deceptive schemes decided; other differences, omission duties, nonrepresentational schemes and unusual recipient preferences remain open. Section 1014’s different Wells construction remains, and purpose to influence under that section is not automatically fraud materiality.

**Holdings navigation:** [Neder v. United States — I. Materiality in the charged mail, wire, and bank fraud schemes](HOLDINGS.md#i-materiality-in-the-charged-mail-wire-and-bank-fraud-schemes-1).

## Standards and Tests selection: Sovereign regulatory licenses and the mail-fraud property requirement

### Sovereign regulatory licenses and the mail-fraud property requirement

**Governing question:** Whether obtaining or renewing a government license by deception targets property under section 1341.

**Current rule:** Authority held by a State solely as sovereign regulator to issue, withhold, renew, regulate or revoke a license is not its property for section 1341. Private value of the permission and continued governmental control do not change that result. The acquisition-by-false-pretenses clause is a method of property fraud, not an independent route dispensing with property in the deceived victim’s hands. Genuine public money and commercially held assets remain within the property requirement; actual loss or reliance is not required by this rule.

**Authority by component:**

- Regulatory character, renewals and victim-property requirement: Canonical Decision Record `Cleveland_v_United_States_merits_2000-11-07.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Sovereign licensing authority is not the State's property; The acquisition clause retains the victim-property requirement, 2000-11-07; Thomas’s unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Cleveland v. United States, 2000-11-07.

**Exceptions and limits:** A license may constitute property in its holder’s hands. Claims directed to unpaid public revenue, genuine commercial assets or a different governmental franchise require their own analysis. The holding does not decide an independent honest-services route or alter the separate materiality element.

**Holdings navigation:** [Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 — Federal fraud offenses and property](HOLDINGS.md#cleveland-v-united-states-531-us-12).

## Standards and Tests selection: Official school worship and independent religious pressure

### Official school worship and independent religious pressure

**Governing question:** Officially organized school worship, delegated representative religious choices and independently coercive school prayer.

**Current rule:** Officials violate the Establishment Clause by selecting clergy, requesting invocations and benedictions, guiding their religious content and incorporating the worship into the official ceremony. Nonsectarian wording and optional attendance do not cure that sponsorship; no separate punishment or quantified-pressure showing is required for this ground. Independently, school-directed clergy prayer is forbidden when the school's control and the occasion's importance place objecting adolescents under substantial pressure to participate, appear to participate or forgo the ceremony. Optional attendance and standing or remaining silent do not necessarily remove that pressure; mere offense is insufficient. The official-sponsorship prohibition also applies when a school organizes, adopts, directs or religiously supervises worship as part of its own event but uses student initiation or delivery or a statutory disclaimer. Those features alone do not make the worship private, and the sponsorship ground remains independent of quantified pressure. The official-worship prohibition also reaches a public university’s selection of a religious leader and incorporation of actual invocation and benediction prayers into commencement. Mature attendance, meaningful freedom to abstain, brevity, nonsectarian language and a sincere secular ceremonial purpose do not cure that official worship; independent clergy composition does not make it private forum speech. Separately, actual pressure to participate in school-directed worship in compulsory or comparably pressured settings violates the Establishment Clause; offense at a genuinely private viewpoint alone does not suffice.

A school may not make an invocation an official representative component of its own ceremony and delegate to a student-majority election whether that component includes religious exercise. Such a mechanism is not transformed into private access by student authorship, optional attendance, possible silence or secular speech, or nonsectarian/nonproselytizing limits. The defect does not require a prayer already delivered or official editing of its words. Genuinely voluntary private prayer, independently chosen student expression, lawful secular messages and neutral private access remain protected; the holding adds no separate religious-pressure test.

**Authority by component:**

- Independently sufficient sponsorship ground: Lee v. Weisman, “Officially organized graduation worship is forbidden”, June 24, 1992; Blackmun's Part II joined by Stone, Stevens, O'Connor and Souter.
- Independently sufficient pressure ground: *Lee*, “The school-directed ceremony also imposes impermissible religious pressure”; Kennedy's concurrence joined by Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor and Souter. Each rule has five direct supporters; neither depends on Marks or on treating Stone as joining Kennedy.

- Ingebretsen v. Jackson Public School District — II. Official school worship cannot be insulated by student delivery or a disclaimer, 1997-03-19; Ginsburg Part II with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer (six) supplies official sponsorship despite student delivery/disclaimer
- Ingebretsen v. Jackson Public School District — III. School-directed worship in a pressured setting is independently forbidden, 1997-03-19; Ginsburg Part III with Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer (six) independently supplies actual-pressure protection

- Official university commencement worship and independent-of-coercion scope: Tanford v. Brand, 1997-12-22; Stone-Zsela Parts II–III with Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; Part I attribution is unanimous.

- Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe; No. 99-62. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, The school may not delegate its official religious choice to a student majority, 2000-06-19; Breyer with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg (seven).

**Present operation effective:** Santa Fe, June 19, 2000, for the official student-majority religious-choice mechanism; Lee, Ingebretsen and Tanford retain their distinct earlier sponsorship and pressure components.

**Exceptions and limits:** Lee applied existing school-worship principles and Lemon's then-independent primary-effect prong at this recurring graduation setting without creating a replacement establishment test. Private prayer and genuinely private equal-access speech remain distinct. Adult legislative prayer, general accommodation, funding and denominational aid retain their distinct rules. Tanford applies the specific-prohibition route of Lemon as Agostini modified it, without a separate coercion finding or an independent primary-effect prong. Other adult ceremonial arrangements, private remarks, nondevotional acknowledgment and silence are not adjudicated.

**Related current rules:** Lemon test states the governing Establishment Clause inquiry as updated in Agostini v. Felton (June 23, 1997, Holding I).

**Holdings navigation:** Lee v. Weisman, 505 U.S. 577 (1992) — Official school prayer. Ingebretsen v. Jackson Public School District (1997-03-19) — First Amendment / Official school worship and private student expression. Tanford v. Brand — Official university commencement prayer.



**Remedial limit:** Relief must address supported unlawful official worship while preserving independently lawful provisions and genuinely private expression; graduation receives no categorical exemption.

## Standards and Tests selection: Equal religious eligibility for controlled secular educational services

### Equal religious eligibility for controlled secular educational services

**Governing question:** Religious-character or religious-location disqualifications within existing programs of independently identifiable secular educational work.

**Current rule:** A State may not exclude a child from consideration for onsite secular special-education service solely because the school is religious where comparable secular locations are permitted and effective public control can preserve the service's secular character. Neutral educational, logistical and fiscal criteria may operate on equal terms. Adequate alternative service does not itself cure that express disqualification.

Religious premises alone do not convert independently controlled, operationally separate public vision service into devotional instruction. Actual safeguards against religious teaching and diversion remain permissible. The establishment permission does not itself require onsite services; the right is to equal consideration within the offered service. Relief must remove the religious criterion while preserving lawful neutral service and site decisions.

For direct institutional grants, an applicant must establish the requested secular work, eligible costs and lawful program compliance under effective use restrictions and reliable accountability. A devotional-financing objection requires a supported operational connection, which may be shown before payment; religious affiliation and hypothetical diversion alone do not establish it. When the work meets the existing program’s lawful requirements and the financing boundary, religious affiliation alone cannot justify denial of equal consideration or payment otherwise required by that program. An express religious disability requires a compelling interest and narrow tailoring, addressing feasible less restrictive means.

**Authority by component:**

- Equal site eligibility and bounded constitutional permission: Canonical Decision Record `KDM_v_Reedsport_School_District_merits_2001-06-25.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. Adequate alternative service does not justify the express religious disqualification; II. Constitutional permission for controlled secular service defeats the categorical separation defense, 2001-06-25; six direct joins.
- Fitted relief and preservation of lawful program criteria: Canonical Decision Record `KDM_v_Reedsport_School_District_merits_2001-06-25.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / III. Relief must remove the religious criterion while preserving lawful service decisions, 2001-06-25; five direct joins.

- Direct secular grants, applicant showing and equal eligibility: Canonical Decision Record `Columbia-Union-College-v-Oliver_merits_2003-04-21.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. Direct grants turn on the work financed; III. Equal eligibility follows within the existing program, 2003-04-21; unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Columbia Union College, April 21, 2003, for direct secular-grant eligibility; K.D.M.’s June 25, 2001 service-site rule and its distinct statutory limits remain.

**Statutory limits:** OAR 581-15-166(1) covers ages three through kindergarten eligibility when parents reject an offered free appropriate public education and choose private schooling; paragraph (2) covers kindergarten eligibility through age twenty-one under the corresponding resident-district offer. Each denies an individual service entitlement in that setting and leaves selection, service and delivery to the responsible public agency under OAR 581-15-171. Paragraph (4) separately requires genuine opportunities for equitable participation consistent with children's number and needs. Those provisions survive subject to equal religious-site eligibility.

**Exceptions and limits:** The service-site rule supplies no individual IDEA right to onsite delivery, automatic specialist order or tuition-reimbursement right; neither component creates a universal private-school subsidy. A materially different service inseparable from devotional instruction remains outside the holding.

**Holdings navigation:** [K.D.M. v. Reedsport School District — Equal eligibility for secular services at religious-school sites](HOLDINGS.md#kdm-v-reedsport-school-district).

## Standards and Tests selection: Public pseudonymity for substantial intimate privacy

### Public pseudonymity for substantial intimate privacy

**Governing question:** Whether a civil litigant may withhold a public name while allowing the opposing party necessary confidential identification.

**Current rule:** Under Rules 10(a) and 26(c), public pseudonymity is permissible when substantial privacy in the action’s intimate subject outweighs the need for public identification and a tailored order preserves meaningful defense access. Keep the proceedings and legal issues public and assess the actual need for confidential identification in the defense; anonymity does not excuse proving the claim.

**Authority by component:**

- Canonical Decision Record `Roe-II-v-Aware-Woman-Center-for-Choice-Inc_merits_2003-06-02.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / III. Public pseudonymity must protect substantial intimate privacy while preserving a fair defense, 2003-06-02; all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Roe II, June 2, 2003.

Source: ../workspace/neutral-projection.md. The following blocks are copied verbatim. All are effective before April 26, 2005. Same-day matters supply no new entering authority to one another.

- **November 9 — [Leocal v. Ashcroft](../records/leocal-v-ashcroft_merits_2004-11-09.md#public-projection).** O'Connor's unanimous opinion excludes an offense permitting accidental or negligent injury without employment of force against another from both parts of 18 U.S.C. §16. Elements and the applicable conviction record govern; injury cannot supply force use, and risk of injury cannot substitute for the specified risk of force use during the felony. A court may decide a disputed criminal predicate before applying the review restriction. The DUI aggravated-felony ground must be removed and continuing immigration consequences corrected through the reviewing court and agency; the convictions remain valid. A recklessness-specific offense is outside the presented question. Bailey and Taylor are applied; Calcano-Martinez is distinguished on its conceded predicates.

- **2005-01-12 — [United States v. Booker](../records/united-states-v-booker_merits_2005-01-12.md#public-projection).** Constitutional rule reaffirmed 6–3; binding Guidelines retained 5–4. Booker sentence vacatur affirmed and remanded, with all nine accepting vacatur once the constitutional premise governs and five supporting the mandatory-framework directions; Fanfan sentence affirmed on the presented challenge, 5–4. A fact legally necessary to increase a binding sentencing ceiling or floor must receive applicable grand-jury charging protection and be proved to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt, validly admitted as an element, or determined beyond a reasonable doubt after a lawful jury waiver. This rule governs present-offense and necessary recidivist facts, including those that increase a binding Federal Sentencing Guidelines range; judicial selection within punishment independently authorized by the verdict or valid admissions remains permissible. The Federal Sentencing Guidelines remain binding to the extent their ranges rest on constitutionally established facts; an unsupported enhancement must be withheld rather than used to replace Congress's mandatory system with an advisory one. Section 3553(b)(1), §3742(e) and the enacted review and remand provisions remain effective in their lawful applications, with judicial discretion exercised within the independently authorized range and lawful statutory departures. Booker's appellate sentence vacatur is affirmed, and his case is remanded for a replacement sentence within a lawfully established binding range, subject to correction of independently established calculation errors. Fanfan's refusal to enhance and resulting 78-month sentence are affirmed against the asserted entitlement to use the excluded findings; any independently preserved calculation issue remains for ordinary disposition. Booker returns for lawful resentencing under the retained binding framework. Fanfan's 78-month sentence stands against the enhancement challenge; any independently preserved calculation question proceeds ordinarily. The Government must identify an independent lawful procedural source before seeking additional enhancement factfinding. Ordinary appellate review continues under the surviving enacted provisions.

- **2005-01-12 — [United States v. Booker](../records/united-states-v-booker_merits_2005-01-12.md#public-projection).** O'Connor, joined by Kennedy and Breyer, dissents from the constitutional holding. Their earlier Angle positions distinguish the statutory offense limits from rules regulating judicial selection within them. Mistretta's institutional sentencing arrangement and the established judicial sentencing role support reconsidering the extension of element protections to those internal constraints. They would permit the challenged judicial findings, reverse Booker's constitutional ruling and return Fanfan for ordinary mandatory-Guidelines sentencing under that preferred rule. They recognize that Angle governs unless reconsidered; they do not treat the federal question as previously unanswered. Breyer's separate Part I explains his additional constitutional position. He finds no coherent logical distinction between a fact raising a mandatory minimum and one raising a maximum, yet opposes extending the element requirement to the sentencing system in either form. That disagreement concerns the constitutional allocation itself rather than an exception consistent with Angle or Harris. In Part II, Breyer is joined by O'Connor, Kennedy and Ginsburg. Given the Court's constitutional holding, they would sever §3553(b)(1), §3742(e) and necessarily incompatible cross-references, preserving guided advisory sentencing. Congress's integrated arrangement relied on judicial assessment of actual conduct and sentencing information beyond charging choices; compulsory ranges rebuilt around jury findings would create disparities and unequal upward and downward operation. They view advisory guidance as the closer surviving statutory design. Courts would remain required to consider the Guidelines and policy statements, offense and offender circumstances, lawful alternatives, seriousness, respect for law, just punishment, deterrence, public protection, effective correctional needs, avoidance of unwarranted disparities and restitution. The sentence would have to be sufficient but no greater than necessary for the applicable statutory purposes, accompanied by reasons and reasonableness review. They would affirm the setting aside of Booker's sentence and resentence him under that system, but vacate Fanfan's sentence for advisory reconsideration even though he suffered no constitutional enhancement error. Ginsburg joins the Court's constitutional rule and this remedial position; the other three retain their constitutional objections.

### 2005-03-30 — [Rhines v. Weber](../records/rhines-v-weber_merits_2005-03-30.md#public-projection)

**Holdings.**

#### Retaining a timely mixed petition during exhaustion

**Holding and operative rule.** A district court may stay a timely mixed petition while the prisoner exhausts state remedies if the prisoner shows good cause for not exhausting first, the unexhausted claims are not plainly meritless, and the record does not show abusive litigation or intentional delay. Good cause means a reasonable explanation in the actual circumstances, not an extraordinary-circumstances or procedural-default test; the court must set reasonable, definite deadlines for seeking state relief and returning to federal court, accounting for delays outside the prisoner’s control.

**Authority.** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join the complete framework. Justice Souter joins the existence of stay power and the merit, anti-abuse and deadline limits, but not the initial good-cause prerequisite.

**Controlling explanation.** Rose v. Lundy gives state courts the first opportunity to decide federal claims. Congress’s exhaustion and limitations rules can serve that purpose while a federal court retains a timely filed action. Landis v. North American Co. supplies ordinary control over pending cases, exercised here within the habeas statutes. Duncan v. Walker excludes time spent in federal court from statutory tolling under §2244(d)(2); retention preserves an existing action rather than supplying a new filing period. Pliler v. Ford left this stay question open while establishing separate protections against particular court-caused filing losses.

The warden correctly argues that routine, open-ended stays would weaken finality and reward premature filing. Cause, a potential-merit screen, exclusion of abuse and definite deadlines answer that objection. Good cause preserves an incentive to exhaust before filing and permits an individualized explanation. Its reasonable-explanation meaning also avoids turning technical uncertainty about exhaustion into a second, rigid procedural-default obstacle. Section 2254(b)(2) permits denial of an unexhausted claim on its merits; it does not compel denial. Relief remains subject to exhaustion, absence of an available state corrective process, circumstances making that process ineffective to protect the applicant’s rights, or counsel’s express waiver of exhaustion for the State, as the statute provides.

Rhines filed with more than eleven months remaining before limitations expired during federal processing. The district court identified eight unexhausted claims and imposed sixty-day initiation and return conditions. Those facts establish the practical importance of stay authority. Actual cause, potential merit, delay and the reasonableness of those conditions require findings under the announced standard.

#### Protecting timely review when applying that discretion

**Holding and operative rule.** Where good cause, potential merit and absence of intentional delay are established and dismissal would defeat timely federal review, denying a stay and dismissing the entire petition ordinarily abuses discretion; the court should retain the action, and any refusal requires a reason compatible with the statute. If a stay is inappropriate, the prisoner must be allowed to delete unexhausted claims and proceed on exhausted claims when whole-petition dismissal would unreasonably impair federal relief.

**Authority.** All nine Justices join this sufficient case for retention and the deletion protection. Justice Souter’s agreement does not make good cause a necessary condition in his separate view.

**Controlling explanation.** The exhaustion requirement directs claims first to the state courts; it does not require destroying a timely federal action whenever the two processes overlap. The filing date and continued pendency therefore matter independently of statutory tolling. A refusal must apply the governing predicates and account for its actual effect on federal review. If retention is unsuitable, deletion preserves the exhausted claims without demanding adjudication of the others. Pliler’s neutral-warning duty retains its particular triggers—an unrepresented prisoner and a qualifying court-directed dismissal election. Rhines had appointed counsel for his amended federal petition, so that duty does not automatically govern his election.

**Precedent Treatment.**

Rose v. Lundy’s total-exhaustion requirement remains operative with bounded stay-and-abeyance in the limitations setting. Duncan v. Walker retains its statutory non-tolling rule; this decision answers the distinct stay question. Pliler v. Ford retains its separate notice, causation, diligence and lawful-remedy rules. Landis v. North American Co. supplies ordinary management authority subject to the governing habeas statutes.

**Law After Decision.**

District courts have a uniform standard for retaining timely mixed petitions while state remedies are pursued. The rule preserves the existing filing and requires prompt exhaustion and return; reopening a terminated action still requires an independently valid procedural ground. The actual stay predicates and reasonable deadlines are matters of application under settled standards, including the deletion protection when whole-petition dismissal would unreasonably impair federal review.




### 2005-04-04 — [Johnson v. United States](../records/johnson-v-united-states_merits_2005-04-04.md#public-projection)

**Holdings.**

#### An order removing a particular predicate is a supporting fact

**Holding and operative rule.** An order vacating the particular state conviction used to enhance a federal sentence is a fact supporting a challenge to that sentence under §2255 paragraph 6(4). The movant must establish the order and its material connection to the asserted current-sentence claim; an actual change in that conviction’s status differs from a new judicial interpretation, repeated legal argument or unsuccessful collateral filing.

**Authority.** Part I of the Court’s opinion is joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation.** The state order changes the legal status of a particular predicate judgment. That event is distinct from the older facts underlying the state challenge. The Government’s argument that only those older facts count would start the period before the state order needed for the present claim exists.

Custis v. United States and Daniels v. United States direct covered attacks on state convictions through their proper review channel and preserve an otherwise authorized later federal application after successful invalidation. Treating the resulting order as fact gives that sequence its actual meaning. Those decisions still require the prisoner to satisfy the independent procedural and substantive requirements for relief from the current sentence.

#### Diligence concerns discovery of the existing order

**Holding and operative rule.** The one-year period under paragraph 6(4) begins when the prisoner could discover the vacatur order through due diligence. The statute requires diligent discovery and filing within one year of that discoverability date; it imposes no additional federal deadline for obtaining a state order that did not yet exist.

**Authority.** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg join Part II’s rule, application and remedy.

**Controlling explanation.** Congress selected discovery of facts supporting the claim. Discovering an existing event and bringing that event into existence are different acts. An order cannot be discovered before it is entered. Clay v. United States preserves attention to the particular statutory timing trigger; the distinct finality and new-right triggers do not supply an unstated procurement condition here.

The Government and dissent argue that a prisoner who initiates state proceedings should not control federal timing through unexplained delay. The concern for finality is substantial, but Congress addressed it through the one-year discovery period and the other restrictions governing collateral relief. State procedural rules govern the state challenge, and the independent federal requirements govern the later sentencing claim. Custis and Daniels establish the proper channel without adding a federal schedule for creating a state judgment. Estimating when a hypothetical earlier state proceeding would have produced relief substitutes a different condition for discovery.

Johnson obtained an order vacating convictions that included a predicate of his career-offender enhancement, then filed federally just over three months later. The categorical timing dismissal therefore cannot stand. Actual discoverability and the order’s material effect on the enhanced sentence require application of the governing rules on remand.

**Precedent Treatment.**

Custis v. United States and Daniels v. United States retain their proper-channel rule and separate prerequisites for a later authorized federal application. This decision determines the previously unresolved vacatur-fact timing question. Clay v. United States preserves the distinct statutory triggers; its ordinary-finality rule remains applicable to the trigger it governs.

**Law After Decision.**

Actual orders changing the status of particular enhancement predicates qualify under the factual-discovery trigger. Diligence is measured by when the order could be learned of, with the movant required to establish discoverability and the order’s material connection to the claim. A later state vacatur thus permits consideration through the enacted timing provision while the independent requirements governing the federal sentence challenge continue to apply.




### 2005-03-30 — [Rhines v. Weber](../records/rhines-v-weber_merits_2005-03-30.md#public-projection)

**Judgment & Remedy.**

**Vacated and remanded, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The pending federal proceeding shall be retained during prompt consideration of whether the actual stay meets the Court’s standard.

**Procedure After Action.**

On remand, the lower courts shall assess Rhines’s actual reason for nonexhaustion, the potential merit of the eight claims, any abusive or intentional delay and his state-court progress. They shall evaluate the existing sixty-day conditions and impose reasonable exhaustion-and-return deadlines if a stay remains warranted. If a stay is refused, Rhines must receive a meaningful opportunity to delete the unexhausted claims where wholesale dismissal would unreasonably impair federal relief. Any dismissal must identify its actual effect on timely federal review.




### 2005-04-04 — [Johnson v. United States](../records/johnson-v-united-states_merits_2005-04-04.md#public-projection)

**Judgment & Remedy.**

**Reversed and remanded, 5–4.**

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, and Ginsburg.
**Opposing:** Justices O’Connor, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer.

The lower court must apply the date on which due diligence would have disclosed the order and determine the vacatur’s material effect on the enhanced sentence under the governing requirements.

**Procedure After Action.**

The case returns for application of the date on which due diligence would have disclosed the order and a reasoned determination of the vacatur’s scope, its connection to the enhancement and the lawful sentencing consequence under §2255. A timing dismissal may not rest solely on failure to obtain the state order earlier. If the authorized claim establishes that the enhancement lacks a required predicate, the sentence must be vacated to that extent and resentencing must proceed under the applicable sentencing law.




### 2005-03-30 — [Rhines v. Weber](../records/rhines-v-weber_merits_2005-03-30.md#public-projection)

**Opinion Topology.**

O'CONNOR, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which STONE-ZSELA, C. J., and STEVENS, SCALIA, KENNEDY, THOMAS, GINSBURG, and BREYER, JJ., joined in full. SOUTER, J., joined except as to requiring an initial showing of good cause and filed an opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment, in which GINSBURG and BREYER, JJ., joined. STONE-ZSELA, C. J., filed a concurring opinion. GINSBURG and BREYER, JJ., also joined the Court’s opinion in full.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer; Souter to the extent stated | Vacatur and remand | All propositions receive nine joins except the necessary initial good-cause condition, which receives eight |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Souter | Ginsburg, Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand | Would omit initial cause; accepts the remaining stay limits |
| Concurrence | Stone-Zsela | — | Joins the Court | Ordinary civil proof of the predicate factual showing |

**Separate Writings.**

Justice Souter, joined by Justices Ginsburg and Breyer, would omit an initial good-cause requirement and focus on demonstrated intentional delay. Exhaustion can be difficult even for courts, and prisoners often lack legal training; a further threshold dispute may consume time without improving protection against abuse. He accepts retention power, the plainly-meritless screen, anti-abuse limits, reasonable deadlines and the judgment. Justices Ginsburg and Breyer share that practical preference while also accepting and joining the Court’s governing reasonable-explanation requirement.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela joins the Court and would expressly require the prisoner to establish the predicate factual showing by the ordinary civil standard. That showing concerns justification and the procedural conditions for retaining the case, with the merits inquiry remaining whether the claims are plainly meritless.




### 2005-04-04 — [Johnson v. United States](../records/johnson-v-united-states_merits_2005-04-04.md#public-projection)

**Opinion Topology.**

SCALIA, J., delivered the opinion of the Court. All nine Justices joined Part I, recognizing the vacatur as a supporting fact. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg joined Part II, adopting discovery diligence alone and reversal. SOUTER, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which O’CONNOR, THOMAS, and BREYER, JJ., joined.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy and Ginsburg in full; O’Connor, Souter, Thomas and Breyer as to Part I | Reversal and remand | All nine join vacatur as fact; five join the discovery-only rule, application and remedy |
| Dissent | Souter | O’Connor, Thomas and Breyer | Would affirm | Procurement-and-discovery rule and its application; joins Part I |

**Separate Writings.**

Souter, joined by O’Connor, Thomas and Breyer, accepts the vacatur as a supporting fact but would require reasonable diligence in obtaining it after entry of the enhanced federal judgment, as well as diligence in learning of it. The federal judgment gives the prisoner a concrete reason to challenge the predicate. Because the prisoner initiates the process producing the new event, the dissent reads the express diligence condition to include reasonable pursuit; state collateral rules do not replace the federal sentence’s separate finality interest.

That rule includes three qualifications. First, delay in state proceedings not attributable to the prisoner after diligent initiation does not defeat the later trigger. Second, when the underlying grounds for the state challenge could not be discovered through diligence until after federal judgment, pursuit is measured from their discoverability, and diligent pursuit permits time to run from notice of the resulting vacatur. Third, even a prisoner whose pursuit was deficient may qualify if the federal motion was filed within one year of the notice date diligent pursuit would have produced.

The dissent would affirm here. Johnson waited from the November 29, 1994 federal judgment until February 6, 1998 to begin the state challenge. Even crediting all time before AEDPA’s April 24, 1996 enactment leaves more than twenty-one months. Limited education, self-representation and waiting for inmate assistance do not explain reasonable efforts or a specific impediment during that interval; the extension request did not pursue state vacatur. On that sequence the dissent concludes that diligent pursuit would have produced notice more than a year before the eventual federal motion, so the third qualification does not save it. Reasonable diligence permits genuine obstacles and does not demand the fastest conceivable action.
